notes:
Slice 'surveillance' (2013–2022, with a few later outcomes of the same cases through 2025): the Snowden disclosures; rights restated in courts and statutes (Google Spain, Schrems I/II, GDPR, Puttaswamy, Carpenter, CCPA/CPRA, LGPD, PIPL, Colorado); the consent-banner era (GDPR application, Planet49, IAB Europe's TCF, Apple's ATT prompt, Google's abandoned cookie plan); scandals and penalties (Equifax, Cambridge Analytica, FTC v Facebook, Clearview AI, Kochava, Meta €1.2bn); and the first person-side signals given legal force (CCPA global-privacy-control rule, Global Privacy Control, Sephora, Colorado's universal opt-out). A 'signals' array profiles the era's four mechanisms (IAB TCF, GPC, ATT, Colorado UOOM) for comparison with IEEE 7012 / MyTerms.

Method: every CONFIRMED quote was captured with tools/fetch-text.py and re-checked with --check (all FOUND at last run). EU texts: eur-lex.europa.eu and curia.europa.eu's judgment viewer block scripted access, so the identical Official Journal and ECR texts were read from the EU Publications Office's Cellar repository (publications.europa.eu/resource/cellar/...; CELEX numbers given in notes); CJEU press releases were read on curia.europa.eu. Some sites refused the helper's user agent (w3.org) — for those, the page was downloaded with curl into the helper's cache and then checked; Brazil's Planalto page is Windows-1252 and was transcoded to UTF-8 before checking. The California leginfo site timed out and was read via the Internet Archive. Non-English quotes (Italian, Portuguese, Chinese) are given in the original with translations in notes.

Could not verify / caveats: (1) California Secretary of State vote counts for Proposition 24 (9,384,625 yes, 56.2%) were read from the Statement of Vote table but the PDF text layer scrambles cells, so that source is PENDING. (2) The Guardian's Verizon story is dated 5 June 2013 by the PCLOB; the Guardian page now shows a later 6 June update timestamp. (3) Apple's newsroom post for iOS 14.5 and Google's Chromium Blog post of 14 January 2020 keep body text in markup the helper cannot extract; they are cited through Apple's developer documentation, the French competition authority and the UK CMA, which quote or date them. (4) Zuboff's definition is quoted via The Observer's review, not from the book itself. (5) Equifax's count changed from ~143 million (company, 7 Sept 2017) to ~147 million (FTC, 2019); both are recorded. (6) 'First public CCPA action' for Sephora rests on law-firm commentary (Arnold & Porter) describing DoorDash as the second.

Known gaps: UK ICO's Clearview fine and its tribunal history; Greece's Clearview fine; the CNIL's €50m Google fine (January 2019; CNIL page removed); the Belgian Market Court's 2025 ruling on the TCF; EU-US DPF challenge (Latombe, General Court) not verified; the NYT's simultaneous Cambridge Analytica report (paywalled, not read); India's DPDP Act 2023 is left to another slice. Web search budget for the session was exhausted part-way, so some leads could not be pursued.

events.title: The Guardian reveals bulk collection of Verizon call records, then PRISM
events.place: The Guardian, Kings Place, London
events.summary: On 5 June 2013 The Guardian published a top-secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court order, granted on 25 April, requiring Verizon to hand the NSA call records 'on an ongoing, daily basis', including domestic calls. On 6 June The Guardian and The Washington Post both reported an NSA programme called PRISM. The Guardian's story drew on a 41-slide training presentation which said the programme let officials collect search history, email content, file transfers and live chats from Google, Facebook, Apple and other US internet companies. Every company that answered the Guardian denied knowledge of it. The US Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board later dated the first story to 5 June 2013 and described it as the first of a series based on documents disclosed by Edward Snowden.
events.significance: Showed that privacy's walls had moved inside the phone network and the cloud, where people could neither see nor object to collection — the grievance that later drove Schrems, the GDPR's enforcement and demands for user-side controls.

He had flown to Hong Kong on 20 May.
events.significance: Put a human face on the gap between what people had agreed to and what was being done with their data, making surveillance a mass public issue across the democracies.

events.title: EU Court of Justice: search engines must delist on request (Google Spain)
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: In Case C-131/12, brought after Mario Costeja González complained in 2010 to Spain's data protection agency about search results linking to 1998 La Vanguardia pages announcing a real-estate auction, the Grand Chamber held that a search engine operator processes personal data and can be obliged to remove links to lawful third-party pages from results for a person's name. It held that the data subject's rights under Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter override, as a rule, both the operator's economic interest and the public's interest in finding the information, unless there are particular reasons, such as the person's role in public life, why the public's interest in access prevails.
events.significance: Established that an individual can make a claim directly against a global platform about how information on them is surfaced — a person-initiated request with legal force, the first widely used 'right to be forgotten'.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 13 May 2014, Google Spain SL and Google Inc. v Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (AEPD) and Mario Costeja González, Case C-131/12, EU:C:2014:317
sources.quote: As the data subject may, in the light of his fundamental rights under Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter, request that the information in question no longer be made available to the general public by its inclusion in such a list of results, it should be held, as follows in particular from paragraph 81 of the present judgment, that those rights override, as a rule, not only the economic interest of the operator of the search engine but also the interest of the general public in finding that information upon a search relating to the data subject’s name.
sources.note: Paragraph 97. curia.europa.eu's judgment viewer blocks scripted access; the identical official text is served by the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62012CJ0131).

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union
sources.title: Press Release No 70/14: Judgment in Case C-131/12 Google Spain SL, Google Inc. v Agencia Española de Protección de Datos, Mario Costeja González
sources.quote: In 2010 Mario Costeja González, a Spanish national, lodged with the Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (Spanish Data Protection Agency, the AEPD) a complaint against La Vanguardia Ediciones SL (the publisher of a daily newspaper with a large circulation in Spain, in particular in Catalonia) and against Google Spain and Google Inc.

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg.

issues: The summary narrows the Court's exception to 'unless the person's role in public life justifies access'. Paragraph 97 says the rule does not apply 'if it appeared, for particular reasons, such as the role played by the data subject in public life', that the interference is justified by the public's preponderant interest. Public role is one example, not the only ground.

Everything else checks out. Paragraph 97 is the right paragraph number. Operative point 3 confirms delisting 'even, as the case may be, when its publication in itself on those pages is lawful'. The press release confirms the 2010 AEPD complaint and the La Vanguardia pages of January and March 1998 announcing a real-estate auction for social security debts.

events.title: Schrems I: the EU Court of Justice strikes down Safe Harbour
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: Maximillian Schrems, an Austrian Facebook user since 2008, complained to the Irish Data Protection Commissioner that, in light of Snowden's 2013 revelations, US law and practice did not offer sufficient protection against surveillance by public authorities of data transferred there. In Case C-362/14 the Grand Chamber declared the Commission's 2000 Safe Harbour decision (2000/520) invalid, holding that laws allowing public authorities generalised access to the content of electronic communications compromise the essence of the right to private life.
events.significance: One individual's complaint knocked out Safe Harbour, the main framework for transatlantic data flows, proving that a person could force the system to answer for where their data goes.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 6 October 2015, Maximillian Schrems v Data Protection Commissioner, Case C-362/14, EU:C:2015:650
sources.quote: In particular, legislation permitting the public authorities to have access on a generalised basis to the content of electronic communications must be regarded as compromising the essence of the fundamental right to respect for private life, as guaranteed by Article 7 of the Charter
sources.note: Paragraph 94. Operative part: 'Decision 2000/520 is invalid.' Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62014CJ0362).

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union

sources.quote: Maximillian Schrems, an Austrian citizen, has been a Facebook user since 2008.

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg.

issues: The summary overstates the complaint as 'US law did not protect data transferred there from surveillance'. The press release says he complained that 'the law and practice of the United States do not offer sufficient protection against surveillance by the public authorities of the data transferred to that country'.

The significance overstates the effect by calling Safe Harbour 'the legal basis for transatlantic data flows'. It was a principal basis, but standard contractual clauses (Commission Decision 2010/87) and binding corporate rules stayed available. The Schrems II press release of 2020 confirms that Decision 2010/87 on SCCs was still in force and valid.
Checks passed: the paragraph 94 quote is verbatim with its number, 'Decision 2000/520 is invalid.' checks FOUND, and the Safe Harbour decision date of 26 July 2000 appears in the press release.

events.title: The GDPR is signed — with a right to object 'by automated means'
events.place: European Parliament, Brussels
events.summary: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation, was signed at Brussels on 27 April 2016 and published in the Official Journal on 4 May 2016, to apply from 25 May 2018. Article 21(5) lets a person exercise the right to object to processing, in the context of information society services, 'by automated means using technical specifications'. Article 25 requires data protection by design and by default, so that by default only the personal data necessary for each specific purpose are processed.
events.significance: Article 21(5) was among the first provisions in a major privacy law to give a person a right that their software can exercise for them, objecting 'by automated means using technical specifications'. It is the legal hook on which machine-readable signals such as Global Privacy Control and person-proffered terms can hang.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation), Article 21(5)
sources.quote: In the context of the use of information society services, and notwithstanding Directive 2002/58/EC, the data subject may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications.
sources.note: EUR-Lex (eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj) blocks scripted access; the identical Official Journal text (CELEX 32016R0679) was read from the EU Publications Office repository.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 25(2) — Data protection by design and by default
sources.quote: The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 99(2) and signature
sources.quote: It shall apply from 25 May 2018.
sources.note: The act closes 'Done at Brussels, 27 April 2016.' The Official Journal header dates publication 4.5.2016.

events.locationNote: The regulation was signed at Brussels; coordinates are the European Parliament's Brussels seat. The Parliament's final plenary vote took place in Strasbourg.

issues: The significance claims that Article 21(5) is 'the first clause in a major privacy law' to anticipate a person's software stating their objection. That 'first' cannot be supported. Recital 66 of Directive 2009/136/EC (the 2009 ePrivacy amendment) already contemplated consent 'expressed by using the appropriate settings of a browser or other application'. California's 2013 amendment to CalOPPA (AB 370) required websites to disclose how they respond to browser 'Do Not Track' signals. Neither is a right to object by automated means, so Article 21(5) may still be the first binding right of its kind, but the unqualified 'first clause' is overstated. EUR-Lex blocked scripted access, so these precedents could not be quote-checked; they are cited only to justify softening the claim.

All factual claims check out: signed 'Done at Brussels, 27 April 2016', OJ L 119 of 4.5.2016, Article 99(2) 'It shall apply from 25 May 2018.', and the texts of Article 21(5) and Article 25(2), with article numbers confirmed in the extracted text. Brussels as the signing place fits the Parliament's Brussels mini-plenary of 27–28 April 2016.

events.title: The European Commission adopts the EU-US Privacy Shield
events.place: European Commission, Berlaymont, Brussels
events.summary: Nine months after Safe Harbour fell, the Commission adopted Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250, finding that the United States ensured an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred to organisations that self-certified under a new EU-US Privacy Shield. The Court of Justice invalidated this decision four years later in Schrems II.
events.significance: A replacement negotiated between governments, not with the people whose data moved — and it did not survive judicial review.

events.title: India's Supreme Court declares privacy a fundamental right
events.place: Supreme Court of India, Tilak Marg, New Delhi
events.summary: In Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, a challenge arising from the Aadhaar biometric identity programme, a nine-judge bench unanimously overruled M P Sharma and, in part, Kharak Singh and held that privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21. The lead opinion by Justice D Y Chandrachud recognised informational privacy, warned that threats come from non-state actors as well as the state, and urged the government to put in place a robust data protection regime.
events.significance: Extended constitutional privacy to the world's most populous democracy. Its opinions explicitly recognised that threats to informational privacy come from private, non-state actors holding data as well as from the state, though they noted that enforcing privacy claims against such actors may require legislation.

sources.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) and Anr. v Union of India and Ors., Writ Petition (Civil) No 494 of 2012 — Order of the Court
sources.quote: (iii) The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.
sources.note: Order of the Court signed by all nine judges, 'New Delhi; AUGUST 24, 2017' (final pages of the 547-page PDF).

sources.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India — judgment of Dr D Y Chandrachud J (for Khehar CJI, Agrawal, Nazeer JJ and himself)
sources.quote: Informational privacy is a facet of the right to privacy. The dangers to privacy in an age of information can originate not only from the state but from non-state actors as well.
sources.note: Same judgment also reads: 'We commend to the Union Government the need to examine and put into place a robust regime for data protection.'

sources.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India — judgment of Dr D Y Chandrachud J
sources.quote: It arises in the context of a constitutional challenge to the Aadhaar project, which aims to build a database of personal identity and biometric information covering every Indian – the world’s largest endeavour of its kind.

events.locationNote: Supreme Court building, New Delhi.

issues: The significance overstates the holding. It says the judgment extended constitutional privacy 'explicitly to threats from private, non-state actors'. The Court's order declares a right under Article 21 and Part III. Chandrachud J's opinion recognises that dangers 'can originate not only from the state but from non-state actors as well' and commends a data protection law to the Government. Kaul J writes: 'The right to privacy is claimed qua the State and non-State actors. Recognition and enforcement of claims qua non-state actors may require legislative intervention by the State.' So the judgment recognised non-state threats but did not make the constitutional right directly enforceable against them.

Checks passed: the Order of the Court overrules M P Sharma outright and Kharak Singh 'to the extent that it holds that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution'. It is signed by all nine judges and dated 'New Delhi; AUGUST 24, 2017'. The order confirms the Chandrachud judgment was delivered for Khehar CJI, Agrawal and Nazeer JJ and himself. Wikipedia independently confirms the 24 August 2017 date and the nine-judge bench.

events.title: Equifax discloses a breach eventually counted at 147 million people
events.place: Equifax headquarters, Peachtree Street, Atlanta
events.summary: On 7 September 2017 the credit bureau Equifax announced that criminals had exploited a website application vulnerability between mid-May and July 2017, initially estimating that about 143 million US consumers were affected; names, Social Security numbers, birth dates and addresses were taken. On 22 July 2019 the FTC announced a global settlement with the FTC, the CFPB and 50 US states and territories of at least $575 million and potentially up to $700 million, putting the number affected at approximately 147 million.
events.significance: Most of the people whose data was taken had never chosen to deal with Equifax at all, a stark case of data held about people without any relationship or terms of their own.

sources.title: Equifax to Pay $575 Million as Part of Settlement with FTC, CFPB, and States Related to 2017 Data Breach
sources.quote: Equifax Inc. has agreed to pay at least $575 million, and potentially up to $700 million, as part of a global settlement with the Federal Trade Commission, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), and 50 U.S. states and territories, which alleged that the credit reporting company’s failure to take reasonable steps to secure its network led to a data breach in 2017 that affected approximately 147 million people.

sources.institution: Equifax Inc. (investor relations, via PR Newswire)
sources.title: Equifax Announces Cybersecurity Incident Involving Consumer Information
sources.quote: Equifax Inc. (NYSE: EFX) today announced a cybersecurity incident potentially impacting approximately 143 million U.S. consumers. Criminals exploited a U.S. website application vulnerability to gain access to certain files. Based on the company's investigation, the unauthorized access occurred from mid-May through July 2017.
sources.note: The initial estimate (143 million) was later revised upward; the FTC settlement uses approximately 147 million.

events.locationNote: Equifax corporate headquarters, 1550 Peachtree Street NW, Atlanta, Georgia.

issues: The significance says people whose data was taken 'had never chosen to deal with Equifax at all'. That is too broad. Equifax's own release says dispute documents for about 182,000 US consumers were accessed, and those people had contacted Equifax. It also says credit card numbers for about 209,000 consumers were taken. Most victims had no direct relationship with Equifax, but not all of them.

Checks passed: 'Released September 7, 2017'. The release gives 143 million, mid-May through July 2017, and 'names, Social Security numbers, birth dates, addresses'. The FTC release gives $575 million, up to $700 million, and approximately 147 million people. Wikipedia independently confirms the upward revision to 147.9 million US consumers.

events.title: Cambridge Analytica: Facebook data of up to 87 million people
events.place: The Observer / The Guardian, Kings Place, London
events.summary: On 17 March 2018 The Observer reported that the political consultancy Cambridge Analytica, which had worked with Donald Trump's election team, had harvested millions of Facebook profiles of US voters to build software to predict and influence voting choices. The data came through a personality-quiz app, 'thisisyourdigitallife', built by the researcher Aleksandr Kogan; about 270,000 people downloaded it, but it also collected information about their friends. On 4 April 2018 Facebook estimated that the information of up to 87 million people, mostly in the US, may have been improperly shared.
events.significance: Showed that one person's 'consent' on a platform could hand over the data of friends who had agreed to nothing — the clearest demonstration that platform-defined consent does not express individual intent.

sources.title: Revealed: 50 million Facebook profiles harvested for Cambridge Analytica in major data breach
sources.quote: The data analytics firm that worked with Donald Trump’s election team and the winning Brexit campaign harvested millions of Facebook profiles of US voters, in one of the tech giant’s biggest ever data breaches, and used them to build a powerful software program to predict and influence choices at the ballot box.
sources.note: The Observer's initial estimate was 50 million profiles; Facebook's later estimate was up to 87 million.

sources.title: An Update on Our Plans to Restrict Data Access on Facebook (Mike Schroepfer)
sources.quote: In total, we believe the Facebook information of up to 87 million people — mostly in the US — may have been improperly shared with Cambridge Analytica.

sources.title: Suspending Cambridge Analytica and SCL Group From Facebook (Paul Grewal)
sources.quote: Approximately 270,000 people downloaded the app. In so doing, they gave their consent for Kogan to access information such as the city they set on their profile, or content they had liked, as well as more limited information about friends who had their privacy settings set to allow it.
sources.note: Company statement, cited for Facebook's own account of the app. Updated 17 March 2018 to say 'The claim that this is a data breach is completely false.'

events.locationNote: The Observer's newsroom at Kings Place, London (shared with The Guardian).

issues: No substantive error. All three quotes were re-fetched and are verbatim. The Guardian page title matches exactly, and the same article names the app 'thisisyourdigitallife' built by 'academic Aleksandr Kogan' and says 'the app also collected the information of the test-takers' Facebook friends'.

The Facebook sources check out. The Grewal post has 'Originally published on March 16, 2018' and 'Update on March 17, 2018, 9:50 AM PT: The claim that this is a data breach is completely false.' The Schroepfer post has article:published_time 2018-04-04. Wikipedia independently confirms 270,000 downloads and up to 87 million users.
Minor context, not an error: The New York Times published its Cambridge Analytica story the same day as The Observer.

events.title: The GDPR applies — and the consent pop-ups multiply
events.place: Brussels (EU-wide application)
events.summary: From 25 May 2018 the GDPR applied across the EU. Consent had to be as easy to withdraw as to give (Article 7(3)), and the most serious infringements became punishable by fines of up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 83(5)). On the first day, the privacy group noyb filed four complaints against Google (Android), Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram over 'forced consent', as 'consent boxes' popped up across the web.
events.significance: Turned privacy from a promise into a liability on the balance sheet — but its most visible product was the consent banner, in which the site, not the person, sets the terms and the choices.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 83(5) — General conditions for imposing administrative fines
sources.quote: Infringements of the following provisions shall, in accordance with paragraph 2, be subject to administrative fines up to 20 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)

events.title: Carpenter v. United States: a warrant for phone location history
events.place: Supreme Court of the United States, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: Using court orders under the Stored Communications Act — which required only 'reasonable grounds', well short of the probable cause needed for a warrant — prosecutors had obtained from wireless carriers 12,898 location points cataloguing Timothy Carpenter's movements over 127 days, an average of 101 a day. In a 5–4 opinion by Chief Justice Roberts, the Court held that the Government's acquisition of Carpenter's cell-site location information (CSLI) was a Fourth Amendment search — deciding no more than that accessing seven days of CSLI is one — and that the government must generally obtain a warrant supported by probable cause before acquiring such records.
events.significance: Cracked the US 'third-party doctrine': data a person generates just by carrying a phone, and that a company holds, can still be the person's private sphere.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.title: Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. ___ (2018), No. 16–402, slip opinion — Opinion of the Court, Part IV
sources.quote: Having found that the acquisition of Carpenter’s CSLI was a search, we also conclude that the Government must generally obtain a warrant supported by probable cause before acquiring such records.
sources.note: Opinion of the Court, Part III-B. 'ROBERTS, C. J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which GINSBURG, BREYER, SOTOMAYOR, and KAGAN, JJ., joined.'

sources.quote: Wireless carriers produced CSLI for petitioner Timothy Carpenter’s phone, and the Government was able to obtain 12,898 location points cataloging Carpenter’s movements over 127 days—an average of 101 data points per day.
sources.note: The syllabus is not part of the opinion; the figures also appear in the opinion.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.title: Carpenter v. United States, No. 16–402, slip opinion — Opinion of the Court, Part I-B
sources.quote: Based on that information, the prosecutors applied for court orders under the Stored Communications Act to obtain cell phone records for petitioner Timothy Carpenter and several other suspects.
sources.note: The orders were issued under 18 U.S.C. §2703(d) ('reasonable grounds'), not warrants.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.title: Carpenter v. United States, No. 16–402, slip opinion — Opinion of the Court, Part IV
sources.quote: That showing falls well short of the probable cause required for a warrant.
sources.note: Refers to the Stored Communications Act 'reasonable grounds' showing.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.title: Carpenter v. United States, No. 16–402, slip opinion — Opinion of the Court, footnote 3
sources.quote: It is sufficient for our purposes today to hold that accessing seven days of CSLI constitutes a Fourth Amendment search.
sources.note: The Court expressly declined to decide whether a shorter period of historical CSLI can be obtained without Fourth Amendment scrutiny.

events.locationNote: Supreme Court Building, 1 First Street NE, Washington, D.C.

issues: Source [0] note locates the quote in 'Opinion of the Court, Part III-B'. In the slip opinion it is the first sentence of Part IV ('IV Having found that the acquisition of Carpenter’s CSLI was a search…'). The source title is corrected to name Part IV.

The summary overstated the holding as 'acquiring cell-site location information (CSLI) was a Fourth Amendment search' in general. The syllabus holds that 'The Government’s acquisition of Carpenter’s cell-site records was a Fourth Amendment search'. Footnote 3 of the opinion says the Court decides no more than that 'accessing seven days of CSLI constitutes a Fourth Amendment search'.

'Without a warrant' is accurate but incomplete. The records were obtained with Stored Communications Act court orders (18 U.S.C. §2703(d)) on a 'reasonable grounds' showing, which the Court said 'falls well short of the probable cause required for a warrant'. The summary now says this.

The 12,898 points, 101 per day and 127 days are from the syllabus and are verbatim. The opinion itself says MetroPCS produced records spanning 127 days and Sprint two more days, 'Altogether … 12,898 location points'. The 127-day span in the syllabus is its own summary. The 5–4 split (Roberts with Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor, Kagan; Kennedy, Thomas, Alito and Gorsuch dissenting) and the decision date of 22 June 2018 are confirmed on the PDF.

events.title: California enacts the Consumer Privacy Act
events.place: California State Capitol, Sacramento
events.summary: Assembly Bill 375, the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, was approved by the Governor and chaptered as Chapter 55, Statutes of 2018, on 28 June 2018. events.title: Shoshana Zuboff's The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
events.place: PublicAffairs (Hachette Book Group), 1290 Avenue of the Americas, New York
events.summary: PublicAffairs published Shoshana Zuboff's The Age of Surveillance Capitalism on 15 January 2019, expanding a concept she had set out in a 2015 journal article, 'Big other: Surveillance Capitalism and the Prospects of an Information Civilization'. Zuboff argued that surveillance capitalism 'unilaterally claims human experience as free raw material for translation into behavioural data', part of which is declared a proprietary 'behavioural surplus' and fabricated into prediction products traded in what she calls 'behavioural futures markets'.
events.significance: Popularised a name for the business model that consent banners were papering over — and framed privacy as a question of who sets the terms for human experience.

sources.title: ‘The goal is to automate us’: welcome to the age of surveillance capitalism (John Naughton)
sources.quote: “Surveillance capitalism,” she writes, “unilaterally claims human experience as free raw material for translation into behavioural data. Although some of these data are applied to service improvement, the rest are declared as a proprietary behavioural surplus , fed into advanced manufacturing processes known as ‘machine intelligence’, and fabricated into prediction products that anticipate what you will do now, soon, and later. Finally, these prediction products are traded in a new kind of marketplace that I call behavioural futures markets .
sources.note: Quotes the book (UK edition spelling); spaces before punctuation are link/italic boundaries in the page text. The book's own opening 'Definition' page was not read online.

sources.title: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism: The Fight for a Human Future at the New Frontier of Power — publisher page
sources.note: The 'On Sale' date shown on the publisher's page for ISBN 9781610395694 (hardcover, PublicAffairs imprint).

sources.quote: Surveillance capitalism challenges democratic norms and departs in key ways from the centuries-long evolution of market capitalism.
sources.note: Last sentence of the article's abstract in the publisher-deposited Crossref record. The title string 'Big other: Surveillance Capitalism and the Prospects of an Information Civilization' is also FOUND on this page. The record gives published-print 2015-03. The SAGE landing page returns 403 to scripts.

issues: The title 'Shoshana Zuboff names surveillance capitalism' overstates the 2019 book. Zuboff introduced the term in 2014–15: the FAZ essay 'A Digital Declaration: Big Data as Surveillance Capitalism' (15 September 2014) and 'Big other: Surveillance Capitalism and the Prospects of an Information Civilization' (Journal of Information Technology 30(1), March 2015). The Crossref record for the 2015 article is added. Foster and McChesney had also used 'Surveillance Capitalism' as a Monthly Review title in July 2014, with a different meaning. The book popularised the term; it did not name it.

Both quotes were re-fetched and are verbatim. Hachette gives 'On Sale Jan 15, 2019' for the PublicAffairs hardcover, ISBN 9781610395694. The Guardian/Observer piece is by John Naughton, published 2019-01-20T07:00Z.

Minor: the summary's quoted words use UK spelling ('behavioural'), taken from The Observer's quotation. The PublicAffairs (US) edition named in the summary spells it 'behavioral'. The wording otherwise matches the book as quoted, and the source note already flags UK spelling.

events.title: FTC imposes a $5 billion penalty on Facebook
events.place: Federal Trade Commission, 600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: The FTC announced that Facebook would pay a $5 billion penalty and accept new restrictions and a modified corporate structure to settle charges that it violated a 2012 FTC order by deceiving users about their ability to control the privacy of their information — including by sharing friends' data with third-party app developers even when those friends had set more restrictive settings. The same day the FTC announced actions against Cambridge Analytica, its former CEO Alexander Nix and the app developer Aleksandr Kogan.
events.significance: The US regulator's largest privacy penalty turned on a simple failure: the company undermined the preferences users had set — the problem that person-set, machine-readable terms are designed to make enforceable.

events.title: Planet49: a pre-ticked box is not consent to cookies
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: In Case C-673/17, brought by the German Federation of Consumer Organisations against Planet49, an online gaming company that had run a promotional lottery, the Grand Chamber held that consent to storing or reading cookies on a user's device under Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive, read with the GDPR, is not validly given by a pre-checked checkbox that the user must deselect to refuse.
events.significance: Defined what the consent banner had to look like — active opt-in — cementing a model in which each site asks and the person answers, one pop-up at a time.

sources.title: Judgment of 1 October 2019, Bundesverband der Verbraucherzentralen und Verbraucherverbände — Verbraucherzentrale Bundesverband eV v Planet49 GmbH, Case C-673/17, EU:C:2019:801
sources.quote: must be interpreted as meaning that the consent referred to in those provisions is not validly constituted if, in the form of cookies, the storage of information or access to information already stored in a website user’s terminal equipment is permitted by way of a pre-checked checkbox which the user must deselect to refuse his or her consent.
sources.note: Operative part, point 1 (interpreting Article 2(f) and 5(3) of Directive 2002/58/EC and Articles 4(11) and 6(1)(a) GDPR). Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62017CJ0673).

sources.note: Describes the parties. The Federation is 'Federal Union of Consumer Organisations and Associations — Federation of Consumer Organisations, Germany'.

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg.

events.title: Google promises to end third-party cookies in Chrome 'within two years' — then doesn't
events.place: Google headquarters, Mountain View, California
events.summary: On 14 January 2020 Google announced that it planned to phase out support for third-party cookies in Chrome within two years, replacing them with 'Privacy Sandbox' tools; the UK Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation and accepted binding commitments. After repeated delays, on 22 July 2024 Google said that instead of deprecating third-party cookies it would offer users a choice, and on 22 April 2025 it said it would not roll out a standalone prompt and would not return to removing third-party cookies. The CMA released Google's commitments on 17 October 2025.
events.significance: Showed that when the browser vendor also runs an advertising business, the person's side of the web cannot rely on the browser alone to set the terms.

sources.quote: On 14 January 2020 Google announced that “… we plan to phase out support for third-party cookies in Chrome. Our intention is to do this within two years.
sources.note: Quotes Google's Chromium Blog post 'Building a more private web: A path towards making third party cookies obsolete' (blog.chromium.org/2020/01/…), whose body text the helper could not extract.

sources.title: A new path for Privacy Sandbox on the web (Anthony Chavez)
sources.quote: Instead of deprecating third-party cookies, we would introduce a new experience in Chrome that lets people make an informed choice that applies across their web browsing, and they'd be able to adjust that choice at any time.
sources.note: Company announcement, cited for what Google itself said it would do.

sources.title: Decision to release the commitments previously accepted by the CMA in respect of Google's Privacy Sandbox proposals

The CMA case page records: 'On 17 October 2025, the CMA issued its Decision to release the commitments.'

issues: No errors found. All three quotes were re-fetched and are verbatim. The CMA notice is dated 11 June 2021 (Case 50972). It records that the CMA opened its investigation on 7 January 2021 and lists '14 January 2020: Google first announced its intent to remove TPCs'.

The CMA release decision is dated 17 October 2025. It confirms that the commitments were accepted on 11 February 2022, and gives the 22 July 2024 blog post and the 22 April 2025 announcement. The Privacy Sandbox post is by Anthony Chavez and dated 2024-07-22.

events.title: Schrems II: the Court of Justice invalidates Privacy Shield
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: On a reference from the Irish High Court in Case C-311/18 — proceedings brought by the Irish Data Protection Commissioner over Max Schrems's complaint against Facebook's transfers of his data to the United States — the Grand Chamber declared Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 on the EU-US Privacy Shield invalid, while holding that the Commission's standard contractual clauses (Decision 2010/87) remained valid. It was the second time a Schrems complaint led the Court to strike down an EU-US transfer framework: in 2015 (Schrems I, Case C-362/14) it had invalidated the Safe Harbour decision.
events.significance: Confirmed that under the GDPR the individual's rights travel with the data, and that no political deal can override them without real redress.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 16 July 2020, Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Ltd and Maximillian Schrems, Case C-311/18, EU:C:2020:559
sources.quote: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 of 12 July 2016 pursuant to Directive 95/46/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on the adequacy of the protection provided by the EU-US Privacy Shield is invalid.
sources.note: Operative part, point 5. Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62018CJ0311).

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union
sources.title: Press Release No 91/20: The Court of Justice invalidates Decision 2016/1250 on the adequacy of the protection provided by the EU-US Data Protection Shield
sources.quote: However, it considers that Commission Decision 2010/87 on standard contractual clauses for the transfer of personal data to processors established in third countries is valid.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union
sources.title: Press Release No 91/20: The Court of Justice invalidates Decision 2016/1250 on the adequacy of the protection provided by the EU-US Data Protection Shield
sources.quote: In a judgment delivered on 6 October 2015, the Court of Justice, before which the High Court (Ireland) had referred questions for a preliminary ruling, declared that decision invalid (‘the Schrems I judgment’).
sources.note: 'That decision' is Decision 2000/520 (Safe Harbour), Case C-362/14. The release goes on to say that Schrems's reformulated complaint concerned transfers under the standard data protection clauses in the Annex to Decision 2010/87.

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg (judgment delivered during COVID-19 restrictions).

issues: The summary's closing line, 'It was Schrems's second successful challenge to the legal basis of EU-US data transfers', is imprecise. The C-311/18 proceedings were brought in the Irish High Court by the Data Protection Commissioner, not by Schrems. Schrems's reformulated complaint targeted Facebook's transfers under the standard contractual clauses, and the Court upheld those clauses. Privacy Shield fell because of the questions the High Court referred. The summary now describes the proceedings accurately and points to Schrems I (6 October 2015, C-362/14, Safe Harbour), with a source added.

Both quotes were re-fetched and are verbatim. The Privacy Shield quote is operative point 5 and the SCC-validity finding is point 4. 'Delivered in open court in Luxembourg on 16 July 2020.' The press release number (91/20) and title are correct.

events.title: California's CCPA rules make browser 'global privacy controls' a valid opt-out
events.place: California Department of Justice, Sacramento
events.summary: The Office of Administrative Law approved the Attorney General's final CCPA regulations, which took effect immediately. Section 999.315(c) required any business collecting personal information online to treat 'user-enabled global privacy controls, such as a browser plug-in or privacy setting, device setting, or other mechanism' signalling an opt-out of sale as a valid consumer request. The California Privacy Protection Agency's 2023 rules re-codified the duty as 11 CCR §7025, 'Opt-out Preference Signals', which gives an HTTP header field or JavaScript object as an example format.
events.significance: The first US rule to require businesses to honour an opt-out signal sent by the person's own software (the GDPR had already let people object 'by automated means using technical specifications') — the direct precedent for honouring machine-readable, person-proffered terms.

sources.institution: California Office of the Attorney General
sources.title: Final Text of Proposed Regulations, Title 11, Division 1, Chapter 20 — California Consumer Privacy Act Regulations, §999.315(c)
sources.quote: If a business collects personal information from consumers online, the business shall treat user-enabled global privacy controls, such as a browser plug-in or privacy setting, device setting, or other mechanism, that communicate or signal the consumer’s choice to opt-out of the sale of their personal information as a valid request submitted pursuant to Civil Code section 1798.120 for that browser or device, or, if known, for the consumer.

sources.institution: California Office of the Attorney General
sources.title: Attorney General Becerra Announces Approval of Final Regulations Under the California Consumer Privacy Act
sources.quote: California Attorney General Xavier Becerra today announced approval by the Office of Administrative Law (OAL) of final regulations under the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA).
sources.note: Same release: 'The approved regulations go into effect immediately.'

sources.title: California Consumer Privacy Act Regulations (final text approved 29 March 2023), 11 CCR §7025 Opt-out Preference Signals
sources.quote: A business that sells or shares personal information shall process any opt-out preference signal that meets the following requirements as a valid request to opt-out of sale/sharing: (1) The signal shall be in a format commonly used and recognized by businesses. An example would be an HTTP header field or JavaScript object.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 21(5) — Right to object
sources.quote: In the context of the use of information society services, and notwithstanding Directive 2002/58/EC, the data subject may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications.
sources.note: An earlier EU provision recognising machine-sent objections. It is cited to qualify the 'first' claim for the California rule.

events.locationNote: California Department of Justice headquarters, 1300 I Street, Sacramento.

issues: The significance line 'The first regulation anywhere to make a signal sent by the person's own software legally binding' overstates. GDPR Article 21(5), in force since 2016 and applicable from 25 May 2018, already provided that 'the data subject may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications'. California's rule was the first US rule of this kind. The GDPR provision is added as a source.

The §999.315(c) lettering was checked and is correct for the approved text. The OAL Amended Notice of Approval in Part and Withdrawal in Part (effective 8/14/2020) withdrew proposed §999.315(c), and the FSOR Addendum says 'the subsequent sections re-lettered accordingly'. The cited PDF, which the AG's CCPA regs page labels 'Final Text of Regulations', is the post-withdrawal text: the withdrawn 'minimal steps' clause is absent and the global privacy control duty is (c).

All three quotes were re-fetched and are verbatim. The CPPA §7025(b)(1) quote was checked in context. The CPPA's rulemaking page confirms: 'On March 29, 2023, the Office of Administrative Law approved the California Privacy Protection Agency’s regulations … The regulations became effective on March 29, 2023.'

events.title: Brazil's General Data Protection Law (LGPD) takes effect

events.summary: Lei nº 13.709 of 14 August 2018, the Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados, names 'informational self-determination' (autodeterminação informativa) among its foundations. After the Senate removed from Provisional Measure 959/2020 an article that would have postponed it, the law entered into force on Friday 18 September 2020; the administrative sanctions of Articles 52–54 applied only from 1 August 2021.
events.significance: Brought a GDPR-style regime, grounded explicitly in informational self-determination, to Latin America's largest country.

events.title: Global Privacy Control launches: a 'do not sell' signal from the browser
events.place: Georgetown University Law Center, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: A coalition spearheaded by Ashkan Soltani (Georgetown Law) and Sebastian Zimmeck (Wesleyan University), with The New York Times, The Washington Post, the Financial Times, DuckDuckGo, Brave, Mozilla, the EFF and others, announced Global Privacy Control, a browser signal communicating a person's 'do not sell or share' request, in answer to California's regulation requiring businesses to honour such controls. events.title: China adopts the Personal Information Protection Law

events.summary: The Standing Committee of the 13th National People's Congress adopted the Personal Information Protection Law at its 30th session on 20 August 2021, with effect from 1 November 2021. events.title: Belgian regulator rules the ad industry's consent framework breaks the GDPR
events.place: Autorité de protection des données / Gegevensbeschermingsautoriteit, Rue de la Presse 35, Brussels
events.summary: The Belgian Data Protection Authority's Litigation Chamber found that IAB Europe's Transparency & Consent Framework — which records users' consent choices from cookie pop-ups in a 'TC String' shared across real-time bidding — failed to comply with the GDPR, that IAB Europe acted as a controller, and fined it €250,000 with orders to fix the framework. On a reference from the Brussels Court of Appeal, the EU Court of Justice held on 7 March 2024 (Case C-604/22) that such a string, capturing a user's preferences, constitutes personal data where it can be associated with an identifier such as an IP address.
events.significance: The industry's machine-readable consent signal was found to breach the GDPR as built — and the Court of Justice confirmed that a string encoding a person's privacy preferences is itself personal data when it can reasonably be linked to an identifier such as an IP address, a principle that bears on any person-proffered terms signal.

events.title: Third attempt: the EU-US Data Privacy Framework
events.place: European Commission, Berlaymont, Brussels
events.summary: After Schrems II, the United States adopted Executive Order 14086 on 7 October 2022, setting new limits and safeguards on signals-intelligence activities and a new redress mechanism for Europeans, complemented by an Attorney General regulation establishing a Data Protection Review Court. myths.claim: Global Privacy Control is just 'Do Not Track' again — a browser flag websites can ignore.
myths.correction: Do Not Track never became a binding standard: the W3C working group concluded its work in January 2019 because there had not been sufficient deployment or planned support, and no privacy statute made honouring it an explicit duty (its one notable legal success came late, when a Berlin district court held in August 2023, in a judgment not final when announced, that under the GDPR a DNT signal is a valid objection). GPC differs in having explicit legal force in some places: California's CCPA regulations require covered businesses to treat it as a valid opt-out of sale or sharing, and in 2022 Sephora agreed to pay $1.2 million to settle the Attorney General's allegations, which included failing to process GPC opt-outs; Colorado has required controllers to honour recognised universal opt-out mechanisms, GPC first among them, since 1 July 2024. Where no such law applies, it remains a request.
